data.text: **Authorization policies** provide a centralized way to express authorization rules in ASP.NET Core.

data.caption: How authorization policies are evaluated
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Incoming Request] --> B{Authenticated?}
    B -->|No| C[401 Unauthorized]
    B --> D{Policy Requirements}
    D -->|Role Check| E[RequireRole]
    D -->|Custom| F[Requirement Handler]
    E -->|Pass| G[200 OK]
    F -->|Pass| G
    E -->|Fail| H[403 Forbidden]
    F -->|Fail| H

terms.definition: A named set of authorization requirements
A single rule that must be satisfied
Evaluates a requirement against the request context
A named group of users, such as Admin or User

data.title: Authorization Policies

cards.title: Policy-Based
cards.description: Centralized rules that can be reused across controllers

cards.title: Role-Based
cards.description: Simple checks against user role claims

data.title: Build an Authorization Policy
data.description: Add a custom authorization policy to a Web API project and protect a controller.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core Web API project
Add a policy called "ManagerOrAbove" that requires the Manager or Admin role
data.expectedOutcome: You can configure and apply authorization policies in your own API.

items.text: Understand the difference between authentication and authorization
Can define a policy with RequireRole
Can apply a policy with the [Authorize] attribute
Know when to use custom requirements vs roles

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use RequireRole for simple role checks
data.takeaway: Policies make authorization maintainable and reusable.
